newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-CAPELLO HAS HIMSELF TO LIVE UP TO AT MILAN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CAPELLO HAS HIMSELF TO LIVE UP TO AT MILAN.

text.p: Newly appointed AC Milan coach Fabio Capello has a difficult act to follow -- Fabio Capello.

The imminent return of Capello to Milan was probably the worst kept secret in European soccer and on Monday, two days after he had won the Spanish league title with Real Madrid, Milan officially confirmed that he would be their coach for next season.
After just one successful year in Spanish soccer, the 51-year-old Capello returns to a happy hunting ground where between 1991 and 1996 he won four league titles and one European Champions Cup.
Capello knows only too well that his brief at Milan is simple -- to take the club back again to the top of world and European club soccer.

"It's useless to try and guess how much I stand to win or lose because Milan has to win and that's that. We start off intending to win", Capello said in an interview with sports daily "Gazzetta Dello Sport" this week.
Capello's second coming at Milan starts from a position of strength.
Eighteen months ago, he opted to leave the club and move to Spain, partly in a fit of pique.
Despite his impressive track record, Milan had proved reluctant to extend his contract, preferring to wait and assess seasonal results.

Since then, Milan has experienced its worst season in a decade, exiting early from both the Champions' League and Italian Cup and finishing only 11th in Serie A and thus out of European competition next season.
Capello's sucessor, Uruguyan coach Oscar Washington Tabarez, failed to last to Christmas.
In early December, Tabarez was replaced by former Italy coach Arrigo Sacchi, a man who like Capello had previously proved a winner on the Milan bench.

Sacchi's second coming at Milan proved a failure since he could not get the team back on course, presiding over some humiliating defeats including a spectacular 6-1 thrashing by newly-crowned champions Juventus at the San Siro.
Capello, too, may be risking his reputation.

When he took over the side in 1991, after a four-year cycle under Arrigo Sacchi, he inherited a talented squad which required a few minor adjustments before quickly refinding its all- conquering stride.
This time, Capello will have to clean out the cupboard, completely reshaping a club which has already bought 10 players for next season.
Furthermore, Capello will be coaching a Milan side that for the first time in nearly 20 years will not build its defence around sweeper and captain Franco Baresi.
Famous names such as Roberto Baggio, Montenegrin Dejan Savicevic and Croat Zvonimir Boban could leave the club this northern summer.
Defender Mauro Tassotti has retired while striker Marco Simone, midfielder Stefano Eranio, Dutch defender Michael Reiziger and French striker Christophe Dugarry are all sure to be heading elsewhere.

"Players like Savicevic and Baggio are on the market but if they don't find clubs they like, they could still stay with us," said Capello. "I told Baggio, and he understood, that the club and I have decided to implement a policy of renewal."

Among the new figures likely to shine in Capello's fresh Milan are Dutch and ex-Ajax Amsterdam striker Patrick Kluivert, due to play alongside Liberian George Weah in an attack of mouthwatering potential.

Other new Milan names are German midfielder Christian Ziege, Dutch defender Winston Bogarde, French midfielder Ibrahim Ba, Piacenza goalkeeper Massimo Taibi, Swedish striker Andreas Andersson and AS Roma midfielder Francesco Moriero.
With any coach other than Capello, the task of blending so many new elements into an immediately winning combination would seem impossible.
However, just one year ago, Capello went to Real Madrid and proved an immediate winner. Bookmakers will not offer long odds against a repeat act in his second coming at AC Milan.
